chunks.text: We'll be live now. So we are on Local Government Port Companies Accountability Amendments Bill. So we got the first 15 minutes for the hearing, the member who carried the bill, Lamanga Solisi. Do we have her here? Yeah. And

I guess you know the rules pretty well. You got 15 minutes. It would be great if you can leave one or two minutes for the members- Sure... of the committee to ask question. And now the floor is yours. I'll just start my timer, Mr. Chair. Yes. Oh.

Well, thank you, Mr. Chair, and members of the Transport and Infrastructure Select Committee for the opportunity to speak to my member's bill. New Zealand has a proud ports and harbors history. The earliest ports were a little more than a few planks leading into the sea. 20th century industrialization has made wharves an impressive landscape of soaring cranes and multicolored containers.

But harbor board politics also had a fiery history as central government established the Chief Marine Board looking after lighthouses, and local government ran trading ports. New settlers were workforce at outports, and town folk from local towns wanted more of a say in development and growth, and sometimes with fiery debates. But ports were impermanent, temporary short-lived due to key characteristics of instability, rudimentary facilities, environment, and economic challenges.

And I tell that story because that's port history in Aotearoa, New Zealand, mid 1800s. This bill is an amendment bill. Because it is a bill that makes sense. And in the first reading, I want to acknowledge all the members who participated in the first reading to this stage. I've been asked to explain the problem definition.

What is that bill aiming to fix? Why has this bill been placed in the member's bill process? And I would like to take this time to take you through that now. The bill is a short bill, as members of the select committee have read. The aim of the bill is to bring transparency and accountability rules into line with Local Government principles.

Public transparency and accountability and awareness of the New Zealand public is important for New Zealand consumers and businesses. And as the committee is aware, New Zealand relies entirely on sea freight for survival, yet there is no national strategy or ports plan.

New Zealand does not have a state-owned or dedicated national merchant shipping fleet for international trade. Our international trade is handled by global shipping, because deregulation in the late 1980s led to the demise of major local carriers.

The government has an unbalanced funding model. Domestic coastal shipping receives zero transport budget, while road freight receives billions. Through this funding model, cargo is forced onto local and nationwide roads, causing congestion and safety risks and pushing our emissions higher.

Foreign ships carry most of domestic sea freight, completely exempt of New Zealand taxes, environmental emission laws, or workers' fair bargaining wage requirements. And because of that, global conflicts, pandemics, and trade disputes have a direct impact on these foreign ships.

For example, the fuel crisis and with impact on vessels that have to come to New Zealand, and that impact may cause industries to shut down. This bill reverses the exclusion of port companies and their subsidiaries from certain rules that apply to council controlled organizations in the Local Government Act 2002.

This will have the effect of applying normal public accountabilities to port companies, including the application of the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987, the requirement to act as a good employer, and the requirement to exhibit a sense of social and environmental responsibility by having regard to the interests of the communities in which they operate.

And Mr. Chair, I would like to thank all the submitters who supported this bill. There were certain themes that came through the submissions, and I want to use some of those quotations. Public accountability. The general feeling from submissions from port companies was there was adequate mechanisms for public reporting and accountability to enable members of the public to set their activities, their strategies, their investments, and so forth, alongside appropriate protections for commercially sensitive information

On the contrary, many other submitters welcome the call for more transparency and easier access to information concerning the operations and governance of port companies as a public right, while at the same time protecting commercial interests that benefit the public.

Collectively however, the majority of submissions from individuals, from unions, iwi, hapū, and businesses, supported the call for increased transparency and public accountability, and I'm just going to quote a few. "The Port CEO Group acknowledges and supports the importance of strong public accountability for port companies." That was from the Port CEO Group.

"This bill recognizes that ports are not merely commercial enterprises, but publicly owned institutions whose decisions have broad public consequences." And that was from the Rail and Maritime Transport Union. And from Ms. Bush, "Ports manage public assets worth billions of dollars. Their decisions affect regional economies, supply chains, and employment.

Large capital projects carry high financial and operational risk. Without transparency, boards and councils cannot make informed decisions." Another theme, good employer, social and environmental responsibility. And I'm grateful that many submitters commented positively about explicit inclusion of these requirements in the bill. From Ms.

Quinn, "Port companies should be subject to the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987, and the requirements to act as a good employer exhibit a sense of social and environmental responsibility by having regard to the interests of the community in which they operate."

That is found in the Local Government Act 2002. From AJ Marshall, "Ports should be held accountable for their actions and practices. They are not above or separate from the law, and the lives and the rights of their workers, tenants, and visitors deserve to be acknowledged in the legal process." We also heard from Forest Owners Association, "We support the bill sets the expectation that port companies have regard to objectives beyond profit. While this was not greatly increased legal constraints on port companies, it sets a norm of

social responsibility and good business practice expected from companies that are all majority owned and some wholly owned by local authorities." From Rail and Maritime Union, "Decisions concerning port investment, land use, safety, employment, and operations have significant economic, environmental, and social consequences, and such decisions should be subject to public scrutiny." A further theme in submission was from local iwi with regards to relationship and restoration. That public accountability, good employer, social and environmental

responsibility are all elements of the bill that were interpreted by several submitters as potential opportunities for restoration and better future gains. From Ms. Rollo, "As Māori, I stand in strong support of the Local Government Port Companies Accountability Amendment Bill.

For too long, publicly owned port companies have used their legal exemption from transparency laws to operate as secretive, profit-driven corporates, completely ignoring their social, their cultural, and environmental impacts on local communities and tangata whenua.

First, this bill gives iwi and hapū a critical legal tool to protect our moana and kaimoana beds. Port activities such as major harbor dredging, construction, and industrial runoff happen directly within our customary and ancestral waters." The Pirira Coal Tribal Authority submission, they requested that the committee note the particular significance of this bill for tangata whenua exercising kaitiakitanga over waterways and coastal environments affected by port operations, and that the explanatory note or parliamentary record explicitly

acknowledge this dimension. Mr. Chair, there are different approaches and proposed alternative and amendments that select committee will consider and decide upon. The key point of difference between submitters was not the intent of the bill, for example, better transparency, public accountability, good employer, social and environment responsibility, but whether the pathway proposed was the best way to achieve it.

Several submissions, including the New Zealand Law Society, Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa, the Port CEO Group, the Rail and Maritime Transport Union, discuss the current legal objective of port companies in Section 5 of the Port Companies Act 1988, which states, "The principal objective of every port company shall be to operate as a successful business." However, the urgency for success without adequate transparency and accountability brought risks according to one submitter, who stated Protect ports from political

interference that prioritises short-term returns over long-term infrastructure resilience. And this submitter stated, "The lack of accountability that leads to waste, inefficiency, and unsafe practices. Ports should not be allowed to hide failures, manipulate reporting, or misleading shareholders and the public." And that was from Ms Bush, who is an ex-employee of Ports of Auckland.

There were a few proposed alternatives that have already been written in the public submissions, and so I won't go through that, but I do want to mention just a quick couple as I wrap up. The Law Society suggested amendments to PCA and Local Government, and if required, the Ombudsman Act, rather than amendments to the Local Government.

And for example, was to amend Section 5 of the LCA to insert any additional principal objectives of port companies, and that's already listed in their written submission. And Forest Owners Association supported greater transparency of port company pricing practices via Local Government and the expectations that companies have regard to objectives beyond profit, and we heard that of the submission last week.

Just as I wrap up, the port strategy is so strategically significant, a type of collaboration that would further encourage closer scrutiny from, and better collaboration between councils on shared cultural, social, economic, and environmental interests and goals. And there were some quotes that were provided already by MUNZ submission.

And so lastly, I do want to thank the Select Committee for hearing my verbal submission, but also, Mr. Chair and members, to the CEOs of the port companies that welcomed me to their sites and provided some really good intel. So thank you. I'm happy to take questions.

Great. Simon, and then Dean. Oh, thank you. Thank you, and thank you for the explanation. Compete with other CCOs, as far as I'm aware. These ports have to compete with other ports for business and trade. And we would all like to better understand the basis of charging and how they make decisions.

But isn't it better that the Local Government process is directed at the port's owner responsible for governance, which in the case of local government, would be the local government entity rather than the port itself? Can I ask something, Chair? Yes. So you're asking me that question?

That's the question. Yeah. The question is, isn't it better that the Local Government process be directed at the port's owner and responsible for governance, which is the local government entities that own the port? Thank you. And in terms of the question that you ask, whilst the committee may feel that it is a better strategy to target my submission or the bill towards port company owners, the public are wanting better accountability and transparency of port activities, and we've heard that loud and clear.

But also, when I visited port company sites, the port CEO group and the CEOs share the same question that you have shared to me. However, I have put back to those CEOs, how do you achieve greater transparency and accountability that the public has a better awareness of if the port companies are not brought under Local Government activities?

Because whilst CEOs explained to me that they have a responsibility to their shareholders and their local community, that was as far as they could see. However, this bill addresses that port companies need to have further public scrutiny and transparency under the Local Government.

But isn't... Sorry, Simon. Just a supplementary. Isn't that up to their owner to determine that? Yes. However, how do you achieve greater transparency if it is not mandated under legislation? All right, Simon. I should come back- Question is really for you.

Sorry, Simon ... as sponsor of the bill. Thank you. Yeah. Not for me, Simon. Not for the committee. All right. Thank you, Simon. Let's move to Dan. A quick one for Dan. Thanks, Limongga, and certainly appreciate the fact that you were listening to the submissions that we heard on this bill. So thank you for your attendance. I guess my colleague has raised, and I've got a supplementary and a primary, but if we take your problem definition, I think there's different ways to interpret the problem definition.

Did you think of other ways to boost accountability and transparency amongst the owners, i.e. the councilors of local authorities? I note that just in Auckland's case, there's CCOs that have been changed to improve accountability to their governing body.

I guess why have we rushed to the Local Government process being changed when have we considered changing the way these organizations are actually accountable to their main owners, which is the governing body? Just throwing out some ideas for you to consider.

One is whether there should be council appointees on port companies. Two is whether ports should be more accountable to their owners. For example, being required to appear before governing bodies on an annual basis, much like select committees do with organizations that come into their remit.

I guess, I'm curious as to whether you've considered other such mechanisms, rather than just the local process, because I think there's been some serious concerns raised around that, so I'm just keen to get your thoughts on that. Appreciate the question.

There have been further considerations as to what is the best legislative tool to achieve the objectives. Certainly, my visits to the ports, with the respective CEOs of the different port companies, shared their personal views as to why they did not support this bill and their concerns around publicly listed companies, for example.

I have looked at a few other, what is the effective tool by way of public accountability or transparency? Many of the CEOs, and I think I visited seven of the port companies, including the three biggest. Oh, sorry, not Littleton, but certainly Auckland, Tauranga. And those CEOs shared that they did not support the legislation because according to them, this was the tool, the current under Port Companies Act was the best tool.

So I questioned them as to what about the accountability and transparency, given the fact that there is no... I don't know if there's other work happening on a nationwide port strategy. You've heard that some of the unions have got concerns in terms of the workers. But certainly with iwi and other individuals like local businesses, we're asking them what is the best tool to get greater transparency and accountability in their view.

So hence some were supporting. Yeah. Some did raise concern in terms of submitters. Yes. That probably might- Yeah, no worries. Just one more supplementary if I can is, have you-- I know you have a government experience at the local level yourself, but have you engaged with councilors and local authorities over this issue to understand what their needs are?

Because they are elected by the people. These assets are held on, really in ownership of local authorities. So I'm keen to get a sense of what feedback you're getting from local elected leaders on their needs in terms of what they think may drive transparency and accountability.

Not as many as I would have liked to, given the time constraint. However, there were a couple in support of better transparency under their local government in terms of Auckland Council, which is quite different. Probably spoke to only one council from the Tauranga area. Okay. Oh, well, thank you, member. The times is up.
Once again, thank you so much for your presentation. Thank you. Thank you. So now we call our next submitter, PTAI. Are we do it online or- Yeah, they're on Zoom. Sure. Heta Gardiner, who's coming.

Hi, how are you? Good. So- Good, thank you... I'm the deputy chair for Transport and Select Committee, oh, Transport and Infrastructure Select Committee today. So, you have 10 minutes, and the floor is yours. Make sure you give us one or two minutes so the members can ask question as well. Thank you. Ka pai. Kia ora tātou. Tēnā koutou e te committee.

Ko Heta Gardiner tōku ingoa. Ko au te kaihautū mō Pirirākau Tribal Authority Incorporated. I appear for Pirirākau Hapū, mana whenua o Ngāhi Ka, whose rohe encompasses the western Tauranga harbor catchments and Te Awanui. Our status is legislated under the Ngā Hapu o Ngāti Ranginui Claims Settlement Act 2025.

Pirirākau strongly supports this bill. This bill targets a structural deficit. Port companies are majority-owned by regional councils through council-controlled holding companies. Port of Tauranga Limited, for example, is 54% owned by Quayside Holdings, the investment arm of Bay of Plenty Regional Council. And this isn't a unique situation to Tauranga. Napier Port, South Port at Bluff, and Marsden Maritime at Northport all share the same structure.

Majority council-owned, NZX-listed, and equally exempt from the accountability frameworks their parent councils must meet. Yet despite that dominant public ownership, port companies have been carved out from the transparency standards that apply to other publicly controlled entities.

That carve out is the anomaly this bill is correcting. Our insistence on this is driven by direct experience. Pirirākau is currently engaged in the FastTrack Approvals Act process for the Port of Tauranga's Stellar Passage development, large-scale dredging and wharf extensions within Te Awanui, Tauranga Harbor. That process exposed an accountability void. Outside of high-stakes capital applicants, there is zero enforceable mechanisms to access background data to fit the port's commercial footprint.

But Te Awanui is a single interconnected system. Sediment and tidal flows do not stop at the edge of a corporate lease. This bill closes three specific gaps. First, Section 74, port companies are currently immune to official information requests under LGOIMA. That's indefensible for entities operating under majority council ownership within public waterways.

LGOIMA access would let us request monitoring data, ecological assessments, and operational records relevant to kaitiakitanga. That is a specific documented need, not a hypothetical one. Second, Section 60A, this stops port companies from locking in major decisions behind closed doors, then presenting communities with the paperwork to rubber stamp it.

Third, Section 59, this provides a statutory framework to challenge the artificial separation between port operations and their environmental consequences. Now, I wanted to talk and to address specifically the commercial risk argument directly. This bill, in our view, does not alter commercial mandates.

LGOIMA already contains robust protections for genuinely commercially sensitive information. Those protections are tested and well understood. If a majority council-owned port can only compete by operating with less transparency than other publicly controlled entities, it's confessing its business model relies on hiding its true cost from the public.

Pirirakau recommends the passing of this bill in its current form, tightened subsidiary coverage to capture all joint ventures and secondary structures, and extended coverage to Section 57 for mandatory community consultation on long-term strategic plans. Port companies operate in public waterways, on publicly owned land, under majority public ownership.

This exemption has no principal justification in our view, and its consequences fall disproportionately on those of us who live with the environmental and cultural effects of port operations daily. For Pirirakau, this is not abstract. It manifests as information asymmetry, accountability gaps- ... and structural barriers to kaitiakitanga.

This bill addresses those consequences directly and proportionately without disrupting commercial operations. Tēnā koutou. Happy to take questions. Thank you. Any members got any questions? We've got a few minutes. Question. I do. Yep. Thank you. Thank you for your submission.

Sorry, I was trying to remember your name, and apologies. Titi Tita. In terms of the transparency, you've clearly outlined and given the sections provided. What else did you want to add in terms of the significance given the Tauranga business case that is upon your iwi at the moment?

I mean, the impact of the activity on the waters is aligned with our very being. Tauranga, te moana o Tauranga, we are a water people, and then we engage with the way in every way of our existence. And so this impacts actually hugely. And so any attempt to increase transparency, which in our view also increases the environmental protections around our waterways, always has a major impact for us.

No doubt. All right, Ken. Now Julia Genter have a question for you. Kia ora. Thanks for your excellent submission. It was very clear. I guess I just wanted to put it to you that we've heard submissions from port CEO representatives and others arguing that they shouldn't have to be subject to LGOIMA, and that it wasn't necessary because they're already regulated in other ways.

I just wondered if you wanted to add anything in response to that. All I would say is I would question the motives of an entity that is encouraging less transparency. That in itself, in my view, was a red flag. If there is nothing to hide, then you wouldn't fear transparency. And so whatever motivates the call for less transparency is certainly something that I would question.

Thank you. We've got a question from Simon. Good afternoon. Thank you for your submission. You talked about hydrogeological or dredging information bathymetry. Is that not information that you can request or seek as part of disclosure from port companies' resource consent applications?

Yeah, it's not straightforward, and there are a number of mechanisms and approaches that we can take to get various bits of information. I guess, the prevailing view, though, is that there is a big gap of transparency and information access that currently exists that has a carve-out that we don't agree with specifically for these port companies, particularly given that they're alignment and often council owned. And so yes, there are--

Mm. We may have some technical- Yes. Stop. We may have some internet issues here. I think we've got an issue with getting information. Yes. Well, maybe if we can get him back online. Yes. He's still online. He just seems to have frozen. He's frozen.

Maybe turn off his camera and- Yes. Oh, yeah. Here's Sir. Yeah. Yep. So just to follow up, so look, I think you made the point that you'd like more disclosure. A follow-up question. Look, if these port companies weren't owned by councils but were private entities, you wouldn't be able to get this information.

Well, this information you say you can't get. So do you think it would be helpful if local government was clear, either they're going to own these things- And they're subject to disclosure, or they're going to privatize them and put them on the same playing field as, say, lines companies or other regulated monopolies.

I don't think it's alignment with our councils or being owned by councils is really the issue. It's the varying rules that we want to address and that we believe this bill addresses. So, that isn't the issue in itself, in our view. So, if they're publicly owned and they're subject to OIA or Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act, you can ask questions.
But if they're privately owned, you can't. So, if they were privately owned, would there still be a problem?

Well, in the absence of absolute transparency, yes. But that's a whole other issue to discuss and explore, right? And what we're arguing here is the current context. And the current context is they are often council owned, and therefore this should be addressed in this way. That is, I think, a whole separate lane and a whole separate discussion.
All right. Thank you so much for your submission today. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Now we call our last submitter for the day. Is it Curry? Kerry. Kerry. Kerry Kunz. Kerry Kunz. Kerry.
Question

Tena koutou. How are you? Good. So, you got five minutes to present your submission, and hopefully you can leave on the two minutes to the members to ask the question as well. So the floor is yours now. Okay. Thank you, Chair. I did a bit of research into this, but I can't cover everything I researched right now. But I think this is a good bill and a needed bill. The ports control major public assets, so greater transparency and accountability are justified.

I understand the concern about commercial sensitivity and political interference, but that is not a reason to avoid accountability. It is a reason to make it precise. Auckland shows exactly why this matters. The proposal was to transfer control of the port's operation to an external party for around 35 years for an estimated 2.1 billion, while the council retained ownership of the land and wharfs.

Thirty-five years is not an ordinary commercial contract. It could bind several generations of councils. That demonstrates the problem. Ownership may remain public while practical control is transferred for decades. My proposal is an amendment, an extra amendment to Section 74B.

It requires one short record stating what control is being transferred, for how long, the key renewal and exit rights, the risks, and the evidence supporting the decision. It protects commercial information, creates no council veto, and leaves the decision with the port board.

It is a narrow safeguard for very large long-term decisions. I ask the committee to seek advice on it. Thank you. Thank you. Has any members got any questions? Yes. Thank you for your sub-- Thanks, Chair. Thank you for your submission. I just wanted to ask you a question quickly about dividend decisions, because you mention it in your written submission.

Yeah. Do you want to explore further or just discuss that further in terms of those dividend, because it is up to currently port companies as to what they land on. But also, the process for those dividend decisions.

I think that there should be accountability for it. Sorry, did I land on the dividend decisions? I was more thinking that the certificate or a record of recording the control of the transfer that's being transferred for how long, the key renewal and the exit rights, the risks, and the evidence supporting the decisions.

Yeah, that would be dividend rights, too, wouldn't it? So yeah, that would all go into that information, and that would be easier to OIA than them saying, "We're not giving you private information." Thank you. Thank you. It seems that we don't have any more question.
So, I just want to say thank you to all the information you prepare. It helps a lot. And thank you for your submission. Thank you. Thank you. Thanks, Kerry.
